A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research pipeline and retain matching benchmark results despite renaming MUSplat to ExtrinSplat. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 has no appendix; v2 includes supplementary Sections 6–10, which were included in the comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original LERF object-selection and ScanNet segmentation results, qualitative comparisons, and component ablations in Tables 2–5.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds sensitivity experiments, runtime measurements, failure analyses, and qualitative evaluations on additional scenes and tasks.

M1.justification: The SAM/DAM2SAM masks, weighted back-projection, entropy/opacity filtering, VLM naming and CLIP matching procedures are retained. v2's extrinsic index layer explicitly organizes the object-to-feature associations and union-based retrieval already described in v1 Section 3.3; it does not establish a changed recognition algorithm.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained LERF and ScanNet evaluations, v2 adds qualitative object extraction on cluttered Grasp-Net scenes and a phone-captured office. It also demonstrates language-directed object removal, translation and stylization, substantially extending evaluated domains and task coverage (Sections 7.3–7.4, Figures 8–10).

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add Occam's LGS, 3DVLGS, Segment-then-Splat, LAGA and LUDVIG to the resource/LERF comparisons. Table 3 adds LAGA and LUDVIG to ScanNet. Earlier comparators remain, substantially broadening comparison against both training-based and training-free methods.

E3.justification: The main LERF and ScanNet protocols are retained. New experimental designs introduce an opacity-only control, mask-view fractions down to 1/32, three VLM choices, descriptor counts of 1/3/5/10, filtering-threshold sweeps and component-level runtime measurements. These are added protocols, rather than evidence that the original benchmark settings changed.

E4.justification: v1's two component ablations are expanded with opacity-only filtering, sparse-mask robustness, VLM and descriptor-count ablations, and threshold sensitivity. v2 also adds runtime profiling, illustrated failures, neutral-point visualization, semantic-category counts and cross-view CLIP similarity analysis (Sections 7–10).

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v2's category-frequency histogram and feature-similarity heatmap add descriptive analyses, without introducing uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark and ablation scores are retained, including 54.3 LERF mean mIoU and 45.5/47.2/53.7 ScanNet mIoU. New baseline entries change comparative rankings: LAGA reports 64.0 on LERF, while the stated 3.9-point lead corresponds to LUDVIG's 50.4. Numerous new outcomes include opacity-only filtering at 52.6, VLM/threshold/descriptor results, 555.14 seconds total processing time, and additional qualitative findings.

T1.justification: The rendering, accumulation, entropy and cosine-similarity mathematics remain equivalent. v2's index notation and Equations 6–7 express the thresholded group selection and union already specified in v1 Section 3.3. No substantive new assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes training-free mask matching and VLM distillation as alternatives to feature optimization. v2 makes an extrinsic paradigm separating geometry from semantics the central contribution, emphasizing overlapping object groups and lightweight semantic indices. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion substantially redefine the claimed conceptual novelty.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of sparse-view failure, VLM dependence, descriptor-induced semantic noise, neutral-point/rendering tradeoffs and memory-constrained parallelization. It expands the retained mask/VLM limitations into concrete failure mechanisms. Section 4.3 also changes the attribution of aggressive foreground removal from entropy-only filtering to opacity-only filtering.

D1.justification: Section 6 newly specifies detection intervals and thresholds, three-view selection, five generated nouns, the exact VLM prompt, matching/filtering thresholds, and ScanNet scene/category lists. Table 9 supplies timing and NVIDIA Tesla V100 hardware information. These substantially improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds related works including LUDVIG, Occam's LGS, VoteSplat and SuperGSeg, and reframes prior approaches as embedding-based rather than uniformly dependent on expensive training. It revises Dr.Splat's description to pretrained product quantization and adds substantive positioning against boundary-refinement approaches in Section 10.1.

P1.justification: The title and method name change, and the abstract, introduction, contribution list, portions of the results discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten around extrinsic semantics. The method gains separate architecture/index-layer subsections, and the supplement organizes implementation, additional experiments, efficiency, failures and discussion.

P2.justification: The document switches from single-column to two-column layout. v1 Figure 1 is removed; its Figures 2–3 are redrawn as v2 Figures 1–2, including an explicit index-layer panel. Tables are expanded and reorganized, and supplementary Figures 5–14 and Tables 6–9 are added. Existing main qualitative comparison images are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reproducibility and validation gaps through explicit implementation settings and prompts, controlled sensitivity studies, measured runtime and concrete failure evidence. These additions make the unchanged method substantially easier to reproduce and assess. However, the unqualified LERF SOTA claim conflicts with Table 2 (54.3 versus LAGA's 64.0), and Section 7.2's zero-opacity-threshold explanation conflicts with Section 3.3's filtering rule. These issues weaken particular interpretations, but the gains in technical transparency and supporting evidence provide a substantial net improvement.
